strengths: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/34e06d0ef9d04ffdb473aaf5d04e9a74/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important problem: evaluating general-purpose software-engineering agents through realistic IDE interaction rather than task-specific interfaces.
PwP appears to be useful infrastructure, combining containerized VSCode instances, execution-based evaluation, checkpointing, multimodal observations, and keyboard/mouse control.
PwP-Bench has unusually broad coverage: 15 tasks, eight languages, multimodal inputs, and activities ranging from repository repair and theorem proving to UI generation and IDE configuration.
The paper evaluates several model families under multiple interface settings and provides informative qualitative examples of grounding, editing, tool-use, and error-recovery failures.
The assisted-tool experiments offer a useful indication that existing agents leave substantial IDE functionality unexploited.
weaknesses: The central empirical message is substantially overstated. Agents restricted to the paper's defining pixel/keyboard/mouse interface achieve at most 10.2% overall, whereas the headline 46.8% result comes from agents given direct file-editing and Bash APIs. Those APIs reintroduce the tool-based interaction that the paper claims PwP can replace, so the strongest results do not establish the main thesis.

Comparisons with prior state of the art are not controlled. The paper averages heterogeneous metrics from different benchmarks and compares a 20-step, 20-example-per-task evaluation against separately reported results using different models, samples, budgets, prompts, tools, and inference strategies. A macro-average over such incomparable scores is difficult to interpret as evidence of approaching or surpassing specialized agents.

PwP-Bench-Lite contains only 20 randomly selected instances per task. The paper supplies no sampling seed, repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance analysis except for one CTF comparison. With binary tasks, one example changes a reported score by five percentage points, making many claimed differences statistically fragile.

The benchmark construction and reproduction details are insufficient. Full per-task instance counts, selection and conversion procedures, prompts, model/API versions, decoding settings, environment images, extension versions, evaluator implementations, and costs are largely absent. Evaluation protocols for the two new task sets are especially under-specified.

The assisted experiment does not isolate learning to use native IDE tools: it exposes manually selected high-level API calls and abstracts each into fixed action sequences. Its gains therefore demonstrate the value of task-specific engineered abstractions, not that an agent can discover or visually operate corresponding IDE functionality.

Several claims exceed the evidence: video and audio support is listed as benchmark multimodality but is not evaluated; access to 'all IDE tools' is asserted without systematic validation; and conclusions that end-to-end computer-use may supersede text-based tools are premature given the severe failure of the primitive-action agents.

There are internal reporting problems. Claude is described as an exception to Set-of-Marks while tables label its input as Screenshot+SoM; Table 4's improvements do not transparently support the stated 'up to 13.3%' average gain; Table 3 contains an incomplete value ('3.%'); and categorical aggregation is not documented precisely enough to reproduce it.

The novelty relative to general computer-control environments and extensible platforms such as OSWorld, WindowsAgentArena, BrowserGym, and OpenHands is presented mostly through feature checklists. More concrete evidence is needed that PwP offers a technically substantive advance beyond an SWE-focused VSCode task suite built on established interaction mechanisms.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/bee38a084c224fee80caf19e1abaee67/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} targets an important problem: evaluating general-purpose agents across diverse software-engineering activities in a common IDE environment.
PwP appears to offer useful infrastructure, including containerized execution, state checkpointing, execution-based evaluation, and support for multiple languages, modalities, and IDE capabilities.
The benchmark aggregates a broad selection of tasks, and the qualitative analysis identifies concrete limitations in visual grounding, file editing, error recovery, and IDE-tool use.
The paper evaluates several major model families and provides per-task results rather than reporting only a single aggregate score.
weaknesses: The central claim is not supported by the primary experiment. Agents restricted to the proposed screenshot/keyboard/mouse paradigm achieve at most 10.2% overall. The reported 46.8% result instead uses direct file-editing and Bash APIs, substantially weakening the argument that pixel-based IDE interaction can replace tool-based agents.

The comparisons with prior state of the art are not controlled. Results use only 20 sampled instances per task, while prior numbers may use different instances, model versions, budgets, tools, prompts, and inference procedures. The authors acknowledge these differences but nevertheless claim comparable or superior performance.

A uniform 20-step limit is especially unfavorable to primitive UI interaction because one mouse or keyboard action accomplishes far less than a file or Bash API call. Consequently, the large performance gap between agent settings cannot cleanly establish the claimed model limitations or paradigm-level conclusions.

The use of Set-of-Marks and parsed interface elements conflicts with the framing of agents operating directly through visual perception. It also introduces ambiguity: the tables label every model as receiving SoM, while the experimental description says Claude is an exception.

The evaluation is statistically weak. Most scores are based on only 20 examples, no repeated runs or confidence intervals are reported, and small differences against prior work are interpreted despite high sampling and agent stochasticity. The lone McNemar test is insufficiently documented and appears difficult to reconcile with cross-study comparisons.

The benchmark construction is under-specified. The paper gives little detail on the two new task sets, instance composition, evaluator validation, contamination or leakage controls, task difficulty, sampling procedure, or whether the Lite subset is fixed and publicly identifiable.

Averaging heterogeneous metrics across datasets—accuracy, visual similarity components, test-generation measures, and normalized competition scores—produces an overall number with unclear meaning. The paper provides no justification or sensitivity analysis for this aggregation.

The assisted-agent analysis reintroduces task-specific, hand-engineered APIs, directly undercutting the paper's critique of such tools. Moreover, the stated 'up to a 13.3%' improvement is inconsistent with Table 4, where several absolute differences are substantially larger.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the manuscript: the code/data release link is blank, and essential details such as full prompts, exact model snapshots, decoding settings, action semantics, seeds, run variance, resource costs, and complete task configurations are missing.

Several claims are overstated, including being the first SWE-focused computer-use environment, supporting any IDE-achievable task, natively supporting all tools, and showing that the prevailing tool-based paradigm may be superseded. The evidence instead shows that current pixel-based agents largely fail and that API access is what makes them competitive.

The paper does not meaningfully discuss security and ethical risks associated with autonomous Bash access, internet-enabled environments, repository manipulation, or offensive-security tasks such as CTF challenges.

strengths: PwP is a timely and meaningful contribution: a unified VSCode-based environment in which agents can address diverse software-engineering tasks through a common observation/action interface.

PwP-Bench has unusually broad scope, combining 15 tasks, eight programming languages, multimodal inputs, and activities beyond code generation, including IDE configuration, refactoring, theorem proving, security challenges, and data science.

The comparison of primitive UI interaction, computer-use augmented with file/bash operations, and task-specific assisted tools yields useful evidence about where current agents fail. The large performance gaps convincingly identify visual grounding, reliable editing, tool discovery, and error recovery as important research problems.
The evaluation covers five prominent model families and reports per-task results rather than only aggregate scores. The qualitative failure cases are concrete and informative.

The environment includes valuable infrastructure features such as sandboxing, execution-based evaluation, parallel containers, checkpointing, and compatibility with existing benchmarks and tool-based agents.
The work could have substantial community value as an evaluation and training platform, assuming the promised code, task configurations, and evaluation harnesses are fully released.
weaknesses: The strongest claim—that one computer-use agent approaches or surpasses specialized state-of-the-art systems—is not established by a controlled comparison. The cited prior results use different model versions, inference budgets, tools, prompts, and sampling protocols; the paper itself acknowledges these discrepancies. Equality of the overall 46.8% averages is therefore not compelling evidence of parity.

The central evaluation uses PwP-Bench-Lite with only 20 examples per task. This is especially fragile for binary success metrics, yet uncertainty intervals, repeated runs, and significance tests are absent except for one InterCode comparison. The assertion that the random subset preserves each task's difficulty is unsupported.

The headline overall average combines heterogeneous quantities—accuracy, visual-similarity measures, normalized competition scores, and averages of multiple submetrics—with equal task weighting. This aggregate is difficult to interpret and can obscure large differences in practical task importance and metric scale.

There is a conceptual mismatch between the motivating pixel-based paradigm and the strongest configuration: the primitive agents receive Set-of-Marks annotations, while the best agents additionally use direct file and shell APIs. Thus, the 46.8% result does not demonstrate software engineering through pixels alone; the genuinely UI-based setting reaches only 10.2%. The terminology around 'computer-use,' 'primitive,' and 'tool-based' agents should be sharpened.

The 20-step cap appears particularly restrictive for repository-level debugging and differs sharply from the budgets used by several compared systems. There is no budget-matched baseline or sensitivity analysis showing how conclusions change with more steps, tokens, wall-clock time, or monetary cost.

PwP-Bench is largely a repackaging of existing datasets, while the two new task collections are described only briefly. The paper lacks sufficient task-generation, annotation, split, evaluator-validation, and contamination/leakage details to assess their quality or reproducibility.

Several causal interpretations are based mainly on qualitative observations. For example, the paper attributes failures to visual grounding and claims training for IDE-tool use would improve performance, but does not systematically annotate failure modes or evaluate a trained intervention. The assisted-agent study changes the action interface and supplies task-specific abstractions, so it provides an upper-bound indication rather than direct evidence about learnability.

The novelty claims are somewhat overstated given general computer-control environments and existing software-agent platforms. The paper would benefit from a more precise account of what is technically new beyond integrating VSCode, benchmark adapters, and evaluation infrastructure.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript: the release link is blank in the anonymized version, exact prompts and agent configurations are not presented, and environment/extension versions, random seeds, failure handling, hardware, runtime, and evaluation costs are not fully documented.

The paper does not meaningfully discuss safety considerations associated with autonomous shell access, optional internet access, security/CTF tasks, or potentially harmful code execution beyond stating that containers are sandboxed.

strengths: The paper introduces a timely and potentially valuable evaluation environment: a containerized VSCode interface in which agents can act through screenshots, keyboard, and mouse while task completion is verified programmatically.

PwP-Bench has unusually broad coverage, combining 15 tasks, 14 programming languages, multimodal inputs, and both conventional coding and non-code IDE activities. The two newly introduced task sets broaden evaluation beyond code generation.

The empirical study covers nine models and three interaction designs. The large gap between visual-only interaction and file/bash APIs is informative, as are the per-task results showing where visual interaction is genuinely used.
The qualitative examples and assisted-tool experiments identify actionable limitations, particularly visual grounding, file editing, error recovery, and failure to exploit IDE functionality.

The environment's Gymnasium-style interface, container isolation, checkpointing, and execution-based verifiers could make it a useful community resource if the claimed release is complete and reproducible.
weaknesses: The central comparison is substantially confounded by the fixed 20-step budget. A file or bash API call can perform work requiring many primitive mouse and keyboard actions, so giving all interfaces the same number of steps systematically disadvantages visual agents. The 250-step experiment covers only three related datasets and actually produces large improvements, reinforcing this concern. Comparisons should control wall-clock time, tokens, cost, or semantic action granularity across the complete benchmark.

The main evaluation uses only 20 examples per task. Consequently, many reported accuracy differences have five-percentage-point resolution and high sampling variance, yet confidence intervals, repeated runs, and statistical tests are almost entirely absent. The claim that this subset preserves the difficulty of the 5,400-instance benchmark is not empirically demonstrated.

A single MiniSweAgent configuration is an inadequate representation of specialized SWE agents. It is not necessarily state of the art across the diverse tasks, and Appendix E acknowledges that stronger specialized systems often score much higher. Thus claims that API-augmented CUAs reach specialist-level performance are overstated.

The overall score macro-averages heterogeneous quantities, including binary accuracy, CLIP-based scores, normalized competition performance, and averages of multiple metrics. These values do not share a common interpretation, and equal task weighting can obscure whether improvements are broad or driven by particular metrics.

Several analyses contain serious internal inconsistencies. The main text attributes grounding errors to GPT-4o and Claude-4.0 at 20% and 95%, respectively, whereas Appendix F reports the reverse. The appendix first says 20 trajectories from two agents but then reports three agents. It also refers to Table 8 as the assisted-agent result even though Table 8 contains the 250-step experiment. These errors undermine confidence in the analysis.

The grounding and failure-mode conclusions rely on very small, manually inspected samples without a clear annotation protocol, multiple annotators, or agreement measurements. Some causal explanations, such as IDE density or insufficient training coverage, remain speculative.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for an agent benchmark sensitive to UI timing and stochastic behavior: prompts, sampling seeds, screenshot resolution, delays, retry policies, environment versions, and full verifier specifications are not adequately documented in the manuscript. The displayed code-release footnote is also empty.

The paper does not meaningfully discuss safety despite executing model-generated commands and adversarial/CTF workloads. Docker isolation is asserted, but the threat model, network policy, resource controls, and handling of untrusted code are not specified.

strengths: The paper asks a timely and practically important question: whether general-purpose computer-use agents can perform realistic software-engineering work through an IDE.
PwP provides useful infrastructure, including a VSCode-based environment, executable verification, Docker isolation, checkpointing, and a Gymnasium-style interface.
The benchmark covers a broad range of languages, modalities, and task families, and the evaluation includes numerous open- and closed-weight models.
The per-task results and qualitative examples expose concrete failure modes such as visual-grounding errors, unreliable file editing, poor recovery, and limited use of IDE functionality.
weaknesses: The main evaluation uses only 20 examples per task and apparently one run per example, despite stochastic inference. No confidence intervals or repeated-run analysis are reported, so many comparisons based on five-percentage-point increments are not statistically convincing.

PwP-Bench-Lite is described as preserving the full benchmark's distribution, but it assigns exactly 20 examples to every task regardless of the original task sizes. The sampled instance identifiers and random seed are also not specified.

The 20-step budget is poorly justified and especially unsuitable for repository-level tasks such as SWE-Bench. File and bash API calls can accomplish much more work per step than primitive GUI actions, making the central comparison sensitive to unequal action granularity. The 250-step experiment covers only three tasks and does not resolve this issue globally.

The specialized-agent comparison is weak: only MiniSweAgent is evaluated uniformly. Claims about approaching specialist-level or state-of-the-art performance rely partly on incomparable published numbers obtained on different subsets, protocols, models, and metrics.

Adding unrestricted file-editing and bash APIs changes the agent interface into something close to an ordinary tool-based coding agent. The resulting improvement does not by itself establish that a general computer-use design matches specialized agents.

The overall score macro-averages heterogeneous quantities such as binary accuracy, CLIP-based similarity, competition-normalized scores, and averages of multiple task metrics. The paper provides little justification for treating these values as directly comparable or equally weighted.

The causal conclusion that visual grounding and failure to exploit IDE tools are the primary bottlenecks is supported mainly by qualitative inspection and small manual analyses rather than controlled ablations. The assisted setting introduces hand-engineered APIs and therefore does not isolate the benefit of better native IDE interaction.

The visual-grounding analysis is internally contradictory: the main text attributes 20% and 95% error rates to GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.0, respectively, whereas the appendix reverses those assignments. The appendix also says it analyzes two agents but reports results for three.

The two newly introduced task collections contain only 20 instances each; General-SWE further divides 20 instances across five distinct activities. This is too small to substantiate broad claims about general software-engineering competence.

Several included tasks, such as HumanEval, do not require substantial or multistep IDE interaction, contradicting the stated benchmark-selection principles and weakening the argument that PwP-Bench consistently measures programming through rich IDE use.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the paper's code-release footnote lacks a usable URL, and exact prompts, sampled instances, verifier details, and sufficient execution configuration are not fully documented.

The manuscript has substantial presentation problems, including inconsistent table/figure references, cramped tables, numerous grammatical errors, and overstrong novelty claims. Overall, the environment is promising, but the current empirical methodology is not sufficiently rigorous for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: Introduces a timely and meaningful evaluation setting: a unified VSCode-based environment for studying whether general computer-use agents can perform realistic software-engineering work.

PwP-Bench is unusually broad, covering 15 tasks, 14 programming languages, multimodal inputs, code generation and editing, data science, theorem proving, IDE configuration, and other non-code SWE activities.

The empirical study evaluates numerous open- and closed-weight models and compares pure visual interaction, file/bash augmentation, a specialized SWE-agent baseline, and assisted tool use. These comparisons yield useful evidence about the importance of interface design.

Programmatic task verification, container isolation, checkpointing, a Gymnasium-style interface, and the stated release of code and data make the environment potentially useful to the wider research community.

The paper provides informative task-level results and qualitative failure analyses. The large gap between pixel-only interaction and file/bash access is a practically important finding, even if its precise magnitude requires more careful measurement.
The additional 250-step experiments partially address the concern that repository-level tasks cannot reasonably be completed under the main 20-step budget.
weaknesses: The principal evaluation uses only 20 sampled instances per task, without confidence intervals, repeated runs, or sensitivity to the sampled subset. With this sample size, a single binary outcome changes many reported task scores by five percentage points, making fine-grained model comparisons unreliable.

The uniform 20-step limit is poorly matched to the highly heterogeneous tasks and interfaces. File edits, bash calls, compound xdotool commands, and visual actions have very different granularity, so equal step counts do not provide an equal computational or interaction budget. The substantial changes in the 250-step results show that this choice materially affects conclusions.

The overall average combines heterogeneous metrics—including accuracy, CLIP-style similarity, normalized competition scores, and averages of multiple submetrics—without calibration. Consequently, claims based on a one-number overall comparison, such as 50.7% versus 48.8%, are difficult to interpret.

The specialized-agent comparison is narrow: the main aggregate comparison uses only MiniSweAgent with one base model. Comparisons with stronger specialized systems are mostly literature numbers evaluated on different subsets and protocols, which the paper itself acknowledges are not directly comparable.

The visual-grounding analysis is based on a very small manually labeled sample and lacks annotation procedures or inter-annotator agreement. It also contains serious internal inconsistencies: the main text reports grounding errors for GPT-4o and Claude Sonnet 4.0 in the opposite direction from Appendix F, while Appendix F says two agents were analyzed but reports three.

Several causal interpretations are stronger than the evidence. Low pixel-only performance may reflect action granularity, observation design, the step budget, prompting, or latency—not only visual grounding and inadequate IDE-tool use. The assisted experiment simultaneously changes the interface and supplies specialized abstractions, so it does not cleanly isolate latent tool-use capability.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete for a benchmark paper: the Lite subset's exact instances or random seed, prompts, trajectory-labeling protocol, per-task resource limits, and evaluation uncertainty are not fully specified in the manuscript.

The paper would benefit from a dedicated limitations and ethics/security discussion, particularly because it includes CTF tasks and agents with bash, software-installation, and repository access, although container isolation mitigates some risk.
